text: People on the far left are, at most, just really f***ing annoying, but people on the far right are genuinely trying to take rights away from women. In the streets, shooting random American citizens, literally kidnapping American citizens and throwing them into detention facilities. There is a very big difference between the two. So the lady in this video essentially claims that there is a very big difference between the far left and the far right. The far left is, at worst, really annoying, while the far right is genuinely dangerous. And yes, she specifically brings up ICE, but I thought, why not look at the bigger picture? Is there actually data on which political extreme is more dangerous, the far left or the far right? As always, we first need to establish what exactly we mean by dangerous. Are we talking about terrorist attacks, riots, property damage, or willingness to use political violence? Because those are not necessarily the same thing. First, terrorism. A 2025 analysis by the Center for Strategic and International Studies examined terrorist attacks and plots in the United States going back to 1994. Historically, right-wing extremists were responsible for substantially more incidents and fatalities. Between 2016 and July 2025, right-wing terrorist attacks killed 112 people, compared with 13 killed in left-wing attacks. But here is something interesting. In the first half of 2025, researchers recorded five left-wing terrorist attacks or plots, compared with just one right-wing incident. It was the first time in more than 30 years that left-wing incidents outnumbered right-wing ones in their dataset. And the newer CSIS report, covering the entire year of 2025, found 21 left-wing versus 9 right-wing terrorist attacks or plots involving anti-government or partisan extremism, resulting in 4 and 3 deaths, respectively. And we can also look at high-profile political attacks. On the conservative side, Donald Trump survived two assassination attempts in 2024. In the first, he was wounded, one rally-goer was killed, and two others were seriously injured. The second was stopped before the attacker could fire at Trump, but he was later convicted of attempted assassination. Then, in September 2025, conservative activist Charlie Kirk was shot and killed while speaking at a university. And in April 2026, another man was charged with attempting to assassinate Trump during the White House Correspondents' Dinner. On the Democratic side, in June 2025, Minnesota politician Melissa Hortman and her husband were murdered. The same attacker repeatedly shot Democratic State Senator John Hoffman and his wife Yvette, but both survived. Two months earlier, someone set fire to Governor George Shapiro's residence while his family was inside. The attacker later pleaded guilty to attempted murder. These attacks were real, but here's the important distinction. Attacking a conservative doesn't automatically make you a far-left extremist, and attacking a Democrat doesn't automatically make you far-right. However, in the cases of Charlie Kirk and Melissa Hortman, CSIS did classify their assassination as left-wing and right-wing partisan terrorism, respectively. Now, what about riots and street violence? The Crowd Counting Consortium, a research project run by Harvard University and the University of Connecticut, tracks political demonstrations across the United States. And according to their data, in 2021 and 2022 combined, there were approximately 25,900 left-wing demonstrations and 10,400 right-wing ones. Participants caused property damage and 191 left-wing events compared with 30 right-wing events. Now, keep in mind, these figures cover all sorts of political demonstrations, not just extremist groups. And the amount of destruction and level of violence matter, too. For example, in 2020, the civil unrest following George Floyd's death cost more than $2 billion in insured losses across the United States in just two weeks. A report by the major cities' chiefs' association also documented more than 2,000 police officers injured across 68 major jurisdictions in the US and Canada in just over two months. For comparison, one of the most prominent examples of violent right-wing protests, the January 6 Capitol riot, resulted in approximately $3 million in estimated damages and related costs, and an estimated 250 injured law enforcement officers. Now, obviously, these are different events covering very different periods. One involved nationwide unrest, while the other was a single-day riot. And the damage figures don't measure exactly the same things. But even if we exclude 2020 entirely and look only at 2021 and 2022, left-wing protests were more frequent, and property damage caused by participants was reported more often, both in absolute numbers and as a percentage of demonstrations. Does that mean far-left extremists are responsible for more violence overall? Not necessarily, because these figures don't tell us how many of these incidents actually involved far-left extremists. Third, willingness to use political violence. And here the research gets particularly interesting, because different surveys produce different results. For example, in 2021, the Public Religion Research Institute found that 35% of Republicans and only 10% of Democrats agreed that American patriots might have to resort to violence to save their country. But by the end of 2025, those numbers had changed to 19% of Republicans and 17% of Democrats. Another survey conducted by Marquette University in September 2025 found that 15% of Democrats and just 6% of Republicans believed political violence could sometimes be justified. And as a cherry on top, according to PRRI's December 2025 survey, 73% of Democrats said right-wing groups were primarily responsible for political violence, while 72% of Republicans said the exact opposite. So these surveys show that attitudes can change over time, and the answers depend heavily on what exactly you are asking. And of course, believing violence can be justified doesn't necessarily mean someone is willing to commit it. And again, these are broader political groups, not specifically far-left or far-right extremists. So what's the conclusion? Well, we can't really give a definitive answer to which political extreme is more dangerous because it depends on what exactly we are measuring. What we can say is that describing the far-left, or the far-right for that matter, as at worst just annoying, is simply wrong. Personally, I oppose radical violence whether it comes from the left or the right. That doesn't mean pretending their records are identical. But telling people that their own side is, at worst, just annoying, is a very convenient way of giving it a free pass. Because once you've convinced yourself that the other side is so much worse, you can start excusing almost anything. Sure, we destroyed property, but look at what they do. Sure, somebody got hurt, but we are fighting the real bad guys. And suddenly, you are no longer asking whether what your side did was wrong. You are just looking for something worse that the other side did.
